 Malaysia’s Haze Is Also A Wildlife Crisis And Demands Digital Solutions

 Opinions on topical issues from thought leaders, columnists and editors. 
 By AP Dr Azian Muhamad Adzmi and Dr Nik Fatinah N. Mohd Farid 
 Malaysia’s recurring haze crisis demands more than emergency responses, school closures and reminders to wear masks.
 Behind the grey skies and deteriorating air quality lies another environmental emergency that receives far less public attention: the destruction of wildlife habitats, the disruption of ecosystems and the growing vulnerability of animals that cannot escape the consequences of forest and land fires.
 As haze from fires in Indonesia, including Kalimantan, affects Malaysia and neighbouring countries, the crisis unfolding in October 2026 should prompt a fundamental question: why does Southeast Asia continue to confront this recurring problem without a sufficiently integrated regional strategy that protects both human health and wildlife?
 The ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre reported transboundary smoke haze across parts of Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo on 19 October, alongside continuing hotspots and dry conditions in parts of the region.
 Malaysia’s authorities have also acknowledged that changing weather patterns alone cannot provide a lasting solution. The underlying causes must be addressed at their source.
--> This is not simply a question of air pollution. It is a question of environmental governance, biodiversity protection and regional responsibility.
 When forests burn, wildlife pays the price 
 Forest and land fires can destroy nesting sites, feeding grounds and breeding habitats. Animals may die directly from flames or smoke, while survivors face food shortages, displacement and increased contact with people.
 In Borneo, species such as orangutans, sun bears and other forest-dependent wildlife are particularly vulnerable when fires damage or fragment their habitats. Displaced animals may move into agricultural areas or settlements in search of food, creating risks for both wildlife and communities.
 The ecological consequences can persist long after the smoke disappears. Damaged habitats may take years to recover, depending on the severity of the fire and the ecosystem involved.
 Repeated burning can further degrade forests and peatlands, weakening their ability to store carbon and support biodiversity.
 The regional haze crisis therefore exposes a fundamental weakness in conventional environmental responses: we often measure success through immediate improvements in air quality, while giving insufficient attention to the ecological damage that continues after the skies clear.
 Malaysia must broaden the definition of recovery. Cleaner air is essential, but genuine recovery must also include habitat restoration, wildlife protection and prevention of future fires.
 Digital technology can turn conservation into prevention 
 One promising approach is to integrate digital innovation with wildlife conservation and community participation.
 Satellite-based fire detection, geospatial mapping, remote sensing and environmental monitoring can help authorities identify fire hotspots, assess potential risks and prioritise field investigations.
 The ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre already provides regional hotspot and smoke-haze information.
 The challenge is to translate available information into timely, coordinated action on the ground.
 For example, a digital conservation platform could combine verified fire alerts, land-use information, wildlife habitat maps and reports from trained field personnel. This would help conservation agencies identify areas where fires threaten ecologically sensitive habitats and direct limited resources towards the locations of greatest concern.
 Artificial intelligence could assist in analysing large datasets, identifying unusual patterns and prioritising potential risks. However, automated alerts must be verified through reliable data and field assessment.
 A satellite hotspot does not, by itself, establish the cause of a fire, identify the responsible party or prove that a particular animal population is threatened.
 Technology must support sound environmental decisions, not replace scientific judgement. Such a system should also be designed around practical needs. Field personnel may work in areas with limited connectivity, while communities may lack access to sophisticated monitoring equipment.
 Mobile reporting tools, offline data collection and accessible dashboards could help bridge these gaps.
 Most importantly, sensitive wildlife-location data must be protected. Publishing precise locations of endangered animals could expose them to poaching or disturbance. Digital conservation must strengthen protection rather than create new risks.
 Conservation requires people, not just platforms 
 Technology alone cannot prevent recurring haze. Fire prevention also depends on land management, effective enforcement, responsible business practices and meaningful community participation.
 This is where communication becomes critical.
 Environmental information does not automatically produce behavioural change. Communities need clear explanations of fire risks, practical reporting channels and confidence that their reports will lead to appropriate action.
 Farmers, plantation workers, local residents, conservation groups and businesses must be engaged as partners in prevention.
 Digital storytelling, local-language educational materials and community-based campaigns can make wildlife conservation more relevant to everyday life.
 Instead of communicating only through dramatic images of burning forests, campaigns should explain the relationship between land clearing, fire prevention, habitat loss and human–wildlife conflict.
 Schools and universities can also contribute through citizen-science initiatives, public education and partnerships with conservation organisations.
 Properly trained participants can document environmental changes and submit observations for scientific verification.
 Yet public participation must not shift responsibility away from governments or businesses.
 Community reporting is a complement to enforcement, not a substitute for it. Those responsible for illegal burning must be investigated through credible evidence and due process.
 Malaysia needs a stronger regional conservation agenda 
 Because smoke travels across national borders, no country can solve the haze problem independently. ASEAN cooperation must move beyond emergency diplomacy towards sustained fire prevention, transparent monitoring and accountability.
 The ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution provides an established regional framework. Its effectiveness, however, depends on implementation, cooperation and the capacity to prevent fires before they escalate.
 Malaysia should continue working with Indonesia and other ASEAN partners to improve information-sharing, coordinate fire prevention and strengthen responses to high-risk areas.
 Regional cooperation should also incorporate biodiversity indicators, including habitat damage, wildlife displacement and restoration progress.
 Businesses operating in agricultural and forest landscapes have an important role.
 Transparent land-use monitoring, effective fire-management plans, traceability and independent verification can help reduce environmental risks.
 Companies should demonstrate how their operations prevent fires and protect biodiversity rather than rely solely on sustainability statements.
 Universities can help connect these priorities. Wildlife scientists can identify ecological risks; digital-technology researchers can develop monitoring and decision-support tools; communication scholars can evaluate public engagement; and engineering specialists can assess the reliability of field systems.
 This multidisciplinary approach could produce practical conservation models that are tested in selected landscapes before wider implementation.
 The real test begins after the haze clears 
 Malaysia cannot control every fire across the region, but it can help strengthen the systems needed to prevent future crises and protect vulnerable ecosystems.
 The immediate priorities are clear: safeguard public health, improve cross-border fire monitoring, investigate illegal burning, protect wildlife habitats and restore damaged landscapes.
 Over the longer term, governments, researchers, businesses and communities must evaluate whether prevention measures actually reduce fires and biodiversity loss.
 The current haze should also be an opportunity to establish a measurable conservation agenda.
 Success should not be judged solely by how quickly the sky becomes blue again, but by whether fewer fires occur, fewer habitats are destroyed and wildlife populations become more resilient.
 The smoke may eventually disperse with changing winds and rainfall. The ecological losses, however, may remain for years.
 If Malaysia and its regional partners continue treating haze primarily as a temporary atmospheric problem, the same cycle of emergency and recovery will persist.
 By integrating digital innovation, scientific evidence and community engagement into regional conservation efforts, Southeast Asia has an opportunity to address the crisis more comprehensively.
 Protecting wildlife is not separate from protecting people. Both depend on healthy forests, responsible land management and institutions willing to act before disaster strikes.
 The next haze season should not find the region asking the same questions again. It should find us better prepared to prevent the fires, protect the animals and hold ourselves accountable for the forests we share.
 -- BERNAMA
 AP Dr Azian Muhamad Adzmi is an Asst Prof at KIMEP University, and Dr Nik Fatinah N. Mohd Farid is a Senior Lecturer at Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM).
